entities.name: PMID:25426055
observations: Study of 30 primary-school children (mean age 10.7 years) using PSG and finger-sequence tapping; better baseline performance associated with fewer slow/more fast spindles and faster slow waves.
Overnight accuracy gain was greatest in children with more slow spindles and slower slow waves, so current skill and overnight gain showed different associations.

entities.name: Sleep frequencies reflect motor skill
observations: In children averaging 10.7 years, better finger-sequence tapping performance correlated with fewer slow/more fast spindles and faster slow waves; greater sleep-related accuracy gain instead occurred with more slow spindles and slower waves.

entities.name: PMID:39804468
observations: In a pediatric Rolandic epilepsy motor-sequence nap study, spindle rate positively predicted sleep-dependent consolidation; each additional spindle/min corresponded to 3.9% greater task improvement (95% CI 1.3–6.4%). This measured spindle rate, not intrinsic frequency.

entities.name: Spindle rate predicts consolidation
observations: In children with Rolandic epilepsy, an additional centrotemporal spindle per minute was associated with 3.9% greater motor-sequence improvement after a nap (95% CI 1.3–6.4%); this supports spindle activity rate, not spindle frequency.
